messages.subject: Silly R.hat issue
parts:
I got weird values for Rhat after I ran 4 chains for 10 iterations each:

Inference for Stan model: turk1_code.
4 chains: each with iter=10; warmup=5; thin=1; 10 iterations saved.

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
a 0.2 0.1 0.6 -0.5 0.0 0.2 0.4 1.1 20 Inf

tau 0.9 0.3 1.1 0.0 0.1 0.3 1.1 2.7 20 Inf

eta[3] -0.1 0.2 0.8 -0.7 -0.6 -0.4 0.2 1.2 20 Inf
eta[4] -0.8 0.1 0.4 -1.4 -1.0 -0.7 -0.6 -0.3 20 Inf
eta[5] 0.4 0.2 1.1 -1.4 0.0 0.8 1.2 1.2 20 Inf
eta[6] 1.1 0.2 0.8 -0.3 0.9 1.5 1.7 1.7 20 Inf
eta[7] 0.4 0.2 0.8 -0.9 0.2 0.6 0.8 1.2 20 Inf
eta[8] 0.0 0.1 0.5 -0.6 -0.5 -0.1 0.3 0.7 20 Inf
lp__ -591361.0 33603.2 150278.2 -763665.2 -723021.8 -578742.8 -447081.9 -444293.3 20 Inf

The problem went away when I did 100 iterations so maybe it's no big deal, hut we should probably fix the function so it does not return Inf's. Perhaps something in the calculation of the variances that implicitly requires some minimum number of draws? (I peeked at the actual simulation draws returned from Stan and they looked fine: no NA's, they took on different values; no 1e-17's, etc.)

messages.author: ab7b24da45678eac
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Silly R.hat issue
parts:
I know Inf as well as NaN could happen.  But I think it is fine: it just means we could not get a sensible rhat.  In the case of total 10 iterations with 5 being warmup, after the splitting, only 2 are in each chain for computing rhats.  So we ends up with Inf (I did not check which step causes an inf though).  

But if we think displaying Inf or NaN is not good, we could change it to NA. 

--
Jiqiang

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Silly R.hat issue (low count boundary conditions)
parts:
On 12/26/12 4:52 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> We could change to NA or even have it default (when it's NA or Inf or Nan) to the number of iterations per chain (5, in
> this case). Or we could have n_eff default to 1. I don't think we want NA's etc because that gets in the way with
> post-processeing.

I'd prefer NaN returns. What post-processing does it screw up?
If it's just visualization in plot(), maybe we should change plot().

What I don't want to do is tell people we have 1 effective sample
(or even worse, tell them we have 5 effective samples), when we
probably don't have any.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Silly R.hat issue (low count boundary conditions)
parts:
Bob
I think n_eff=1 might be some sort of minimum. If you'd prefer, we can have it return n_eff=.1. Currently it's returning n_eff=10 which isn't right at all. In general I don't want to be returning NA's or Nan's. These are not really NA's or Nan's; we just have a particular formula for R.hat and n.eff that we haven't adapted to work with chains of length 5. That's fine--I don't think we need to kill ourselves coming up with a definition that works with chains of length 5, but when it doesn't work, I'd rather have it report a number that clearly represents DOES_NOT_CONVERGE (e.g., Rhat=5 and n_eff=1 (or, if you'd prefer, n_eff=0.1). I guess what I'm saying is, this is not a 0/0 situation. It's just a situation where we have not gone to the trouble of being super-cereful in the definition of R.hat, and I think it makes more sense to kluge it by giving R.hat a large value, than to kluge it by returning NA or Nan.
A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Silly R.hat issue (low count boundary conditions)
parts:
I understand that it's OK to have a piecewise
estimator that does different things for different
sample size.

I'm just saying I'm uncomfortable over-estimating something
like effective sample size. Could we just make R-hat
equal to infinity and n_eff = 0? Those are at least
not NaN values.

I still don't understand what post-processing you need
an R-hat value for and n_eff value for if we don't have
any effective samples yet.

- Bob
